The papers that made the modern mind.

Fourteen waves of works — spanning twenty-six centuries. Wave 14 goes to the deepest unifiers: the seven universal principles that, once understood, unlock thousands of facts across physics, biology, mathematics, philosophy, and contemplative traditions. The variational principle (Fermat, Bernoulli, Euler, Lagrange, Hamilton), Noether's symmetry-conservation bridge, information-as-substrate (Bekenstein, Wheeler, Susskind), hierarchy (Simon, Salthe), complementarity (Bohr, Heisenberg), dependent origination (Buddha, Nagarjuna, Dogen, Huangbo), via negativa (Pseudo-Dionysius, Eckhart, Nicholas of Cusa, John of the Cross) — plus the deepest questions: why anything at all exists (Parmenides, Heidegger, Whitehead, Tillich, Sartre) and the problems of qualia (Husserl, Merleau-Ponty, Nagel, Jackson, Levine, McGinn). Each entry is given in four voices: the version a curious child can hold, the counter-intuitive flash that connects to today, the version a sharp A-level student deserves, and the version a doctoral examiner would accept.

About the four layers

Every paper carries four layers, written so that the same idea reaches you at whatever altitude you're standing on today.

Wave 1 (31): foundational papers in AI-adjacent fields. Wave 2 (62): broader categories — ancient studies, theology, anthropology, architecture, music, film, astronomy, geology, chemistry, medicine. Wave 3 (51): truly universal ideas — one sentence unlocks thousands. Wave 4 (48): AI and neural networks in depth. Wave 5 (25): the originals — forgotten founders, pre-prints, original equations. Wave 6 (22): hidden foundations — pre-modern originals. Wave 7 (25): forgotten first authors — papers that already had the answer decades before the field got credit (Cauchy, de Moivre, Laplace, Linnainmaa, Ivakhnenko). Wave 8 (25): the untranslated originals — Soviet preprints, Italian doctoral theses, UK Ministry reports, French posthumous books (Lyapunov 1892, Monge 1781, Kotelnikov 1933, Manin 1980, Wiesner 1983). Wave 9 (25): the genuinely unread — unpublished memos, Spanish ring networks, French cybernetics, Soviet probability in Italian journals (Pitts 1942, Lorente de Nó 1938, Hayek 1952, Khachiyan 1979, Glivenko 1933). Wave 10 (25): the universal sentences — papers where one sentence unlocks thousands of things (Carnot 1824, Gauss 1827, Galois 1832, Hardy 1908, Bell 1964, Wolpert 1996). Wave 11 (25): number theory & primes — the deepest laws about the integers (Fermat 1640, Euler 1740, Riemann 1859, Hadamard 1896, Selberg 1949, Green-Tao 2008, AKS 2002). Wave 12 (24): the most universal principles — meta-laws that unlock thousands of things (Aristotle, Leibniz, Maupertuis, Hume, Kant, Comte, Mill, Peirce, Frege, Russell, Wittgenstein, Popper, Cox, Jaynes, Spencer-Brown, Anderson, Bak, Prigogine). Wave 13 (23): the deepest meta-principles — self-reference, fixed-points, conservation of information, autopoiesis, strange loops (Brouwer, Banach, Tarski, Kleene, Wigner, Feynman, Landauer, Conway, Wilson, Hofstadter, Maturana & Varela, Bennett, Chalmers, Clark & Chalmers, Watts & Strogatz, Barabási & Albert, Rao & Ballard, Friston, Varela, Deacon, Russell). Wave 14 (25): the deepest unifiers — the seven universal principles that unlock thousands of facts: variational (Fermat, Bernoulli, Euler, Lagrange, Hamilton), Noether's symmetry-conservation, information-as-substrate (Bekenstein, Wheeler, Susskind, Brillouin), hierarchy (Simon, Whyte, Salthe), why anything at all exists (Parmenides, Heidegger, Whitehead, Tillich, Sartre), and the problems of qualia (Husserl, Merleau-Ponty, Nagel, Jackson, Levine, McGinn). Default: Wave 14.

  • Elementary — one vivid sentence, no jargon, true to the heart of the idea.
  • ⚡ Aha — the counter-intuitive flash that connects the paper to your life today.
  • Abitur — what a sharp A-level / Abitur student should walk away with after a thoughtful reading.
  • PhD — the precise claim, the technical apparatus, and the non-obvious consequence.

Curated to complement (not duplicate) the asanAI course. PDFs link to public archives where possible; some links point to publisher pages where the original is paywalled.
